name: Right-wing populism
summary: Right-wing populism, in the scholarship on the populist radical right, is populism (a pure people against a corrupt elite, politics as the people's general will, impatience with institutions that constrain it) joined to nativism, the demand that the nation be made up of its natives, and to authoritarianism. The defining scholarship names this core and little else, so most economic, social and foreign-policy positions vary between parties and are not part of the ideology.
scope: The populist radical right as Cas Mudde and Cristobal Rovira Kaltwasser define it: a core ideology that combines nativism, authoritarianism and populism, found in Europe (Fidesz, the Austrian Freedom Party) and elsewhere. Positions that parties of the family differ on, or that only a leader's speeches or a party's platform state, are not part of the ideology and are left null. Left-wing populism, historical agrarian populism and the broader populism are other subjects.

sources.author: Cas Mudde
sources.usedFor: Defines the populist radical right (nativism, authoritarianism, populism) and reports its positions on immigration, crime, democracy, the economy, Europe and globalization.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: All the parties want more policemen with better equipment and more prisons with stricter regimes (p. 146).

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: Almost all populist radical rightists accept assimilation of non-nationals, which they call integration, within one official national culture (Leitkultur), and reject multiculturalism (p. 144-145).

bypass-parties-groups.rationale: Populist democracy shows aversion to intermediate bodies, seen as artificial divisions or special interests, and the parties call for personalised politics and breaking the established parties' monopoly (pp. 151, 153).

conscription.rationale: Most parties support compulsory military service as a civic duty, although some oppose it (p. 150).

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: In the populist idea the general will cannot be limited by anything, not even human rights or constitutional guarantees, so populists defend extreme majoritarian democracy; the party literature itself often stresses an independent judiciary (pp. 23, 154-156).

death-penalty.rationale: Many parties call for the death penalty, notably for terrorism and major drug dealing, and only a few are openly against it (p. 147).

democracy-best.rationale: The populist radical right is not antidemocratic in a procedural sense: its leaders say there is no alternative to democracy, though they want to change its rules (pp. 138, 151).

direct-votes.rationale: Virtually all populist radical right parties call for the introduction or increased use of referendums, many wanting every major decision open to the voice of the people (pp. 151-152).

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Nativism, the family's key feature, holds that non-native persons and ideas are fundamentally threatening to the homogeneous nation-state (p. 19).

empower-international-orgs.rationale: The populist radical right distrusts international organizations such as the EU and the UN, and fears globalization as a threat to the nation-state (pp. 74, 196).

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Populism puts nothing above the general will, not even human rights or constitutional guarantees, and rejects pluralism and minority rights (pp. 23, 155-156; Mudde and Rovira Kaltwasser, ch. 5).

ethnic-nation.rationale: Mudde defines nativism, the core of the family, as the view that states should be inhabited exclusively by members of the native group, which is defined on ethnic, racial or religious grounds with always a cultural component; most parties settle for an ethnocracy (pp. 18-19, 139-144).

experts-over-public.rationale: Populist ideology reveres the common sense of the people and sets the pure people against the corrupt elite (p. 23).

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: Most populist radical right parties reject the sale of native land to foreigners, as in Hungary, Bulgaria and Poland (p. 128).

free-trade.rationale: Many parties are close to national capitalism, in which the market is accepted but international free trade is largely rejected (p. 125).

gender-social-construct.rationale: The parties stringently defend the natural differences between the sexes and oppose the equalization of the feminists (p. 92).

islam-incompatible.rationale: Mudde reports that populist radical right parties argue Islam is incompatible with liberal democracy or European civilization and that Muslims can never assimilate unless they give up Islam (p. 145).

legalize-drugs.rationale: The parties campaign against any attempt to tolerate or legalize drugs, and many call for the death penalty for major dealers, with only a few favouring liberalized distribution to addicts (pp. 147-148).

minority-language-support.rationale: The parties oppose special facilities for cultural minorities and call for eliminating state support of cultural pluralism, for example against Turkish in the Bulgarian school curriculum (p. 145).

nation-first.rationale: For the family the economy should be at the service of the nation and only the nation, and globalization and supranational bodies are rejected as threats to the independence of the nation-state (pp. 123, 196).

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: The parties have great difficulties with minority rights within their state and oppose special facilities for cultural minorities, which they see as hindrances to assimilation (pp. 145, 149).

one-party-rule.rationale: Most parties are careful not to cross the line between democracy and dictatorship, though a few leaders have called for authoritarian rule (pp. 145-146, 150).

open-borders.rationale: Nativism holds that non-natives threaten the homogeneous nation-state, and the family's slogans ("Own people first") and calls to close borders to immigrants are incompatible with open borders (pp. 19, 139, 149).

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: The key internal enemy of all populist radical right parties is the elite, criticised as traitors to the nation and corruptors of the people, and the core ideology pits the pure people against the corrupt elite (pp. 22-23, 65-66).

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Most parties hold negative views of the European Union and have given up on it since the 1990s, although most still favour some looser form of European cooperation (pp. 159, 181-182).

preserve-national-culture.rationale: For nativists culture is a rigid category that must be preserved and cultivated, and the parties proclaim strengthening the own culture a national priority (pp. 144-145).

reduce-immigration.rationale: Nativism treats non-natives as a threat to the homogeneous nation-state, and the parties are vehemently xenophobic towards non-European immigrants, calling for expulsion of illegal aliens and for closing borders to Muslim immigrants (pp. 19, 70, 139, 149).

rehabilitation.rationale: The family holds that the protection of society must rate higher than the rehabilitation of the criminal, and demands tougher laws, longer sentences and stricter prisons (p. 147).

separated-powers.rationale: Populism is essentially a monist ideology, inherently opposed to division and pluralism, and holds the primacy of the political over other forces (pp. 151, 154-155).

social-market-economy.rationale: Virtually all parties accept capitalism and the market economy, and support the welfare state in principle for the needy of the own nation (pp. 122-123).

strong-leader.rationale: Most parties call for increased powers of the main political figure, a president or premier, some for a superpresidential system (pp. 153-154).

surveillance-ok.rationale: The populist radical right believes the state should no longer be obstructed in defending against aliens and terrorists by principles like the right to privacy or legal counsel (p. 155).

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: The parties hold economic protectionism, singling out small businesses and agriculture for national protection (pp. 125-127).

traditional-family.rationale: The family shares a minimalist consensus of patriarchal family values, treating women's politics mainly as family politics and defending the natural differences between the sexes (pp. 92-93).

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: Welfare chauvinism is the family's nativist model of the welfare state: benefits go to the native needy and aliens are excluded, with national preference in social services, jobs and housing (pp. 130-132).

work-for-welfare.rationale: The parties want to exclude those who can work but prefer to live off the state (Sozialschmarotzer) and reserve provisions for those who really need them (pp. 124, 131).

missingStatements.text: Welfare benefits should be reserved for citizens rather than extended to immigrants.
missingStatements.rationale: Welfare chauvinism, expanding welfare only for those deemed fit to receive it, is a documented feature of the family.

notes: Searched: the defining scholarship (s5, s6, s7; Mudde's book chapters 1 and 3 to 8) for each theme (government, society, world, economy, liberty, culture, means). It states the core (nativism, authoritarianism, populism) and, for democracy, rejection of constraints on the popular will; s6 says even Euroscepticism and opposition to immigration no longer set the family apart from mainstream right parties. Earlier answers drawn from Wikipedia, Trump's 2017 inaugural address and Orban's 2014 speech were nulled: a leader's speech is not the ideology's defining source, and parties of the family differ on economics, religion and family law.
